meta.title: GET /v1/ – API service metadata
meta.descriptionHTML:
GET /v1/ – API service metadata

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Service discovery: Clients can find out what version of the API is running without needing prior knowledge.
  • Integration testing: Automated tests can verify the service is responding correctly before running full test suites.
  • Documentation access: Developers can quickly locate the interactive API documentation and metrics endpoints.
  • Environment awareness: Operations teams can confirm which environment (dev, staging, prod) they're working with.
  • Without this endpoint, clients would have to guess URLs or hardcode configuration, making the API harder to discover and integrate.

What it does:

  • Returns basic service information: name, version, runtime environment.
  • Provides links to interactive documentation and metrics endpoints (when enabled).
  • Useful for service discovery, health inspection, and integration tests.

Access:

  • Public endpoint (no authentication required).
  • Anyone can call this to discover the API.

Behavior:

  • No caching: Always returns fresh metadata.
  • Environment-aware: Shows current APP_ENV (dev/staging/prod).
  • Feature detection: Links to /v1/docs and /metrics only when enabled in config.

Responses:

  • 200 OK: Returns service metadata JSON.

Examples:

# Check API metadata
curl https://api.example.com/v1/
# → {"service": "cineca-agentic-platform", "version": "0.1.0", "env": "dev", "docs": "/v1/docs", "metrics": "/metrics"}

health.title: GET /health/live – Check if the application process is running
health.descriptionHTML:
GET /health/live – Check if the application process is running

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Crash detection: Container orchestrators (Kubernetes, Docker Swarm) need a quick way to detect if the app has crashed or frozen.
  • Automatic restart: When this endpoint fails, orchestrators automatically restart the container to restore service.
  • Resource efficiency: A fast, lightweight check prevents unnecessary resource usage in monitoring systems.
  • Uptime monitoring: Health monitoring tools use this to track service availability and trigger alerts.
  • Without this endpoint, orchestrators can't distinguish between a slow app and a crashed one, leading to poor failure recovery.

What it does:

  • Returns a simple plain-text ok string to confirm the process is alive.
  • Designed for container orchestrators (Kubernetes, Docker, Nomad) to verify the app hasn't crashed.
  • Performs no external network calls or expensive checks (responds instantly).

Access:

  • Public endpoint (no authentication required).
  • Typically called by infrastructure (load balancers, orchestrators).

Behavior:

  • Lightweight: No database queries, no Redis checks, no I/O operations.
  • Fast response: Should respond in <1ms under normal conditions.
  • Plain text: Returns text/plain (not JSON) for minimal overhead.
  • Always 200: Never returns errors (if we can run this code, we're alive).

Responses:

  • 200 OK: Returns plain text ok (process is alive).

Examples:

# Check if app is alive
curl https://api.example.com/v1/health/live
# → ok

health.title: GET /health/ready – Check if the service is ready to accept traffic
health.descriptionHTML:
GET /health/ready – Check if the service is ready to accept traffic

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Traffic routing: Load balancers need to know which instances can safely handle requests before sending traffic.
  • Graceful deployment: During deployments, new instances report 'not ready' until dependencies are available, preventing user errors.
  • Dependency validation: Confirms that databases, caches, and other services are reachable before accepting requests.
  • Operational control: Operators can manually mark an instance as 'not ready' for maintenance without killing it.
  • Without this endpoint, load balancers might send traffic to instances that can't process requests, causing cascading failures and user errors.

What it does:

  • Performs dependency checks on critical components (PostgreSQL, Redis, Memgraph).
  • Returns aggregate status: ok (ready), degraded (partial), or error (not ready).
  • Provides per-dependency details for troubleshooting (connection errors, timeouts, etc.).
  • Used by load balancers to decide if instance should receive traffic.

Access:

  • Public endpoint (no authentication required).
  • Typically called by infrastructure (load balancers, health checkers, deployment tools).

Behavior:

  • Dependency checks: Tests PostgreSQL, Redis, and optional Memgraph connectivity.
  • Status aggregation: ok if all pass, degraded if some pass, error if critical components fail.
  • Fallback mode: When HEALTH_ALLOW_MG_HEALTH_FALLBACK=1, missing Memgraph adapter is non-fatal (degraded, not error).
  • Admin control: Readiness can be toggled via admin endpoint (for graceful draining).

Responses:

  • 200 OK: Service is ready (all checks passed or degraded with fallback policy).
  • 503 Service Unavailable: Service is not ready (critical dependencies failed).

Examples:

# Check if service is ready
curl https://api.example.com/v1/health/ready
# → {"service": "cineca-agentic-platform", "status": "ok", "time": "2025-10-09T12:34:56Z", "checks": {...}}

# Check when dependencies are down
curl https://api.example.com/v1/health/ready
# → 503 {"status": "error", "checks": {"postgres": {"ok": false, "error": "connection refused"}, ...}}

health.title: GET /health/components – List health status of all system components
health.descriptionHTML:
GET /health/components – List health status of all system components

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Comprehensive monitoring: See health of all components (databases, caches, queues, observability) in one request.
  • Operator dashboard: Provides complete system snapshot for monitoring dashboards (Grafana, Datadog, etc.).
  • Troubleshooting: Quickly identify which specific components are unhealthy without checking each individually.
  • Standardization: Replaces multiple legacy endpoints (/health/db, /health/redis, etc.) with unified interface.
  • Without this endpoint, operators need multiple requests to check all system dependencies.

What it does:

  • Probes all registered components in parallel.
  • Returns individual status for: app, postgres, redis, memgraph, providers, workers, ollama, prometheus, grafana.
  • Each component reports: ok, status, latency_ms, details.
  • Always returns HTTP 200 (reports status even when some components failing).

Access:

  • Public endpoint (no authentication required).
  • Typically called by monitoring systems and operator dashboards.

Behavior:

  • Parallel probing: All components checked simultaneously for minimal latency.
  • Never fails: Always returns 200 with individual component statuses.
  • Timeout enforcement: Each probe has hard timeout (200-500ms).

Responses:

  • 200 OK: Returns component health summary (even if some failing).

Examples:

# Check all components
curl https://api.example.com/v1/health/components
# → {"service": "...", "checks": {"postgres": {...}, "redis": {...}, ...}}

health.title: GET /health/components/{name} – Check health of a single component
health.descriptionHTML:
GET /health/components/{name} – Check health of a single component

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Focused monitoring: Check specific component without querying all dependencies.
  • Alert targeting: Monitoring systems can create component-specific alerts.
  • Debugging: Quickly verify if a specific component is the root cause of issues.
  • Performance: Faster than /health/components when only one component matters.
  • Without this endpoint, monitoring systems must parse full component list for single checks.

What it does:

  • Probes a single component by name.
  • Returns: ok, status, latency_ms, details.
  • Available components: app, postgres, redis, memgraph, providers, workers, ollama, prometheus, grafana.
  • Always returns HTTP 200 (reports status even if component failing).

Access:

  • Public endpoint (no authentication required).
  • Typically called by monitoring systems for component-specific checks.

Behavior:

  • Single probe: Only checks requested component.
  • Never fails: Always returns 200 with component status.
  • Timeout enforcement: Probe has hard timeout (200-500ms).
  • Unknown components: Returns error status if component name invalid.

Responses:

  • 200 OK: Returns component health (even if component failing).

Examples:

# Check PostgreSQL
curl https://api.example.com/v1/health/components/postgres
# → {"ok": true, "status": "ok", "latency_ms": 12}

# Check Redis
curl https://api.example.com/v1/health/components/redis
# → {"ok": true, "status": "ok", "latency_ms": 3, "details": {"queues": {...}}}

health.title: GET /health/startup – Diagnostic startup health check
health.descriptionHTML:
GET /health/startup – Diagnostic startup health check

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Deployment validation: CI/CD pipelines need to verify all dependencies are available before declaring a deployment successful.
  • Troubleshooting: When deployments fail, this endpoint provides detailed error messages showing exactly which dependency is unavailable.
  • Migration verification: Confirms that database migrations have completed before accepting traffic.
  • Rate limit validation: Verifies rate limiting is configured correctly (e.g., RATE_LIMIT_MODE=prod in production).
  • Semantic clarity: Distinguishes startup checks (one-time validation) from ongoing readiness checks (continuous monitoring).
  • Without this endpoint, deployment scripts would have to guess whether failures are temporary (retry) or permanent (rollback), leading to longer outages.

What it does:

  • Returns comprehensive health information including all readiness checks.
  • Includes: Rate limit configuration diagnostics (mode, backend, limits).
  • Includes: Migration state and enforcement policy.
  • Includes: Environment diagnostics.
  • Surfaces detailed dependency errors for troubleshooting during provisioning.
  • Intended for deployment automation and troubleshooting.

Access:

  • Public endpoint (no authentication required).
  • Typically called by deployment tooling (CI/CD, provisioning scripts).

Behavior:

  • All readiness checks: Tests PostgreSQL, Redis, Memgraph, providers, workers.
  • Rate limit config: Reports current RATE_LIMIT_MODE and actual rate limit values.
  • Migration verification: Confirms migrations applied if ENFORCE_MIGRATIONS=1.
  • Production validation: Verifies RATE_LIMIT_MODE is 'prod' (not 'test') in production.

Responses:

  • 200 OK: Service dependencies are healthy (ready for traffic).
  • 503 Service Unavailable: Dependencies failed or not ready (deployment should retry).

Examples:

# Check startup health during deployment
curl https://api.example.com/v1/health/startup
# → {"service": "cineca-agentic-platform", "status": "ok", "environment": {"rate_limit_mode": "prod", ...}, ...}

# Diagnose startup failures
curl https://api.example.com/v1/health/startup
# → 503 {"status": "error", "environment": {...}, "checks": {...}, "migrations": {"required": true, "applied": false}}

auth.title: GET /auth/me – Get your user information from token
auth.descriptionHTML:
GET /auth/me – Get your user information from token

Why we need this endpoint:

  • User interface personalization: Front-end apps need to display the current user's name and permissions to customize the UI.
  • Permission checking: Client apps verify what actions the user can perform before showing buttons or menu options.
  • Token validation: Developers can quickly check if their token is valid and contains the expected scopes.
  • Debugging authentication: When users report permission errors, this endpoint confirms what the token actually contains.
  • Without this endpoint, client apps would have to decode JWT tokens themselves (insecure) or show generic UIs that don't reflect user permissions.

What it does:

  • Returns information extracted from your current Bearer token.
  • Shows your username (token subject), granted scopes, roles, and computed permissions.
  • Useful for client-side UI to display current user or for token inspection/debugging.

Access:

  • Requires valid Bearer token in Authorization header.
  • Any authenticated user can call this to see their own token claims.
  • Requires user:me or admin:all scope.

Behavior:

  • Rate limited: Max 30 requests per 60 seconds per user.
  • Token parsing: Extracts sub, scopes, roles, and computes effective permissions.
  • No caching: Always returns fresh token claims (no conditional GET).

Responses:

  • 200 OK: Returns UserInfo with token claims.
  • 401 Unauthorized: Missing or invalid Bearer token.
  • 403 Forbidden: Token lacks required scope (user:me or admin:all).
  • 429 Too Many Requests: Rate limit exceeded (>30 requests/minute).

Examples:

# Get your user info from token
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN' \
  https://api.example.com/v1/auth/me
# → {"sub": "user123", "scopes": ["user:me", "jobs:read"], "roles": ["developer"], "permissions": ["jobs:read", "user:me"]}

admin-tenants.title: Why we need this endpoint:
admin-tenants.descriptionHTML:
GET /v1/admin/tenants – Retrieve all tenants in the platform

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Platform administrators need to see all registered tenants to monitor the system
  • Essential for tenant management and auditing who has access to the platform
  • Without it, admins would have no way to discover which organizations are using the system
  • Helps identify configuration issues across multiple tenants

What it does:

  • Fetches a complete list of all tenant organizations registered in the platform
  • Returns tenant details including ID, name, admin email, metadata, and timestamps
  • Supports pagination to handle large numbers of tenants efficiently
  • Includes caching to improve performance for repeated requests

Access:

  • Only administrators with admin:all scope can call this endpoint
  • Regular users cannot list all tenants (security isolation)

Behavior:

  • Pagination: Returns up to 100 tenants per page (configurable 1-1000)
  • Caching: Supports If-None-Match header - returns 304 if data hasn't changed
  • Headers: Includes ETag for cache validation and Link header for next page
  • Performance: ETag-based caching reduces bandwidth and server load

Responses:

  • 200 OK: Successfully retrieved tenant list (may be empty if no tenants exist)
  • 304 Not Modified: Your cached copy is still valid (ETag match)
  • 401 Unauthorized: Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 403 Forbidden: User lacks required admin:all scope

Examples:

# List first 100 tenants
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"

# List with custom page size
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants?page_size=50" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"

# Get next page using pagination token
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants?page_size=100&page_token=eyJvZmZzZXQiOjEwMH0" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"

# Conditional request with caching (prevents re-downloading if unchanged)
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
     -H 'If-None-Match: "page-hash-abc123"'

admin-tenants.title: Why we need this endpoint:
admin-tenants.descriptionHTML:
POST /v1/admin/tenants – Register a new tenant organization

Why we need this endpoint:

  • New organizations need to be onboarded to the platform
  • Creates isolated environments for different companies or teams
  • Without it, there's no way to add new customers or departments to the system
  • Essential for multi-tenant architecture and proper data isolation

What it does:

  • Creates a new tenant with a unique server-generated ID
  • Validates tenant information (name, admin email, optional metadata)
  • Stores tenant configuration for future operations
  • Supports idempotent retries (safe to call multiple times with same data)

Access:

  • Only administrators with admin:all scope can create tenants
  • Requires X-Tenant-Id header for audit trail (which admin tenant created this)

Behavior:

  • Auto-generated ID: Server creates unique tenant ID (format: tenant-xxxxxxxx)
  • Idempotency: Calling with identical data returns existing tenant (200 OK, not 201)
  • Conflict detection: Returns 409 if tenant name exists with different configuration
  • Validation: Checks email format, name length, and required fields

Responses:

  • 201 Created: New tenant successfully created (includes Location header)
  • 200 OK: Tenant already exists with exact same configuration (safe retry)
  • 401 Unauthorized: Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 403 Forbidden: User lacks required admin:all scope
  • 409 Conflict: Tenant name exists but with different email or metadata
  • 422 Unprocessable Entity: Invalid email, missing fields, or validation errors

Examples:

# Create a new tenant
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -H "X-Tenant-Id: tenant-admin-root" \
     -d '{
       "name": "ACME Corporation",
       "admin_email": "admin@acme.com",
       "metadata": {
         "region": "us-east-1",
         "tier": "premium"
       }
     }'

# Create tenant with minimal fields (metadata optional)
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{
       "name": "Startup Inc",
       "admin_email": "contact@startup.io"
     }'

# Idempotent retry (returns 200 OK if exact match exists)
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{
       "name": "ACME Corporation",
       "admin_email": "admin@acme.com",
       "metadata": {"region": "us-east-1", "tier": "premium"}
     }'

admin-tenants.title: Why we need this endpoint:
admin-tenants.descriptionHTML:
GET /v1/admin/tenants/{tenant_id} – Retrieve a specific tenant's details

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Administrators need to view complete details of a specific tenant
  • Required for verifying tenant configuration and troubleshooting
  • Without it, you'd have to list all tenants and filter manually (inefficient)
  • Enables direct access to tenant information for API integrations

What it does:

  • Fetches detailed information for one specific tenant by its ID
  • Returns all tenant properties: name, admin email, metadata, timestamps
  • Provides ETag header for efficient caching
  • Validates that the tenant exists before returning data

Access:

  • Only administrators with admin:all scope can access tenant details
  • Regular users cannot view tenant information

Behavior:

  • Direct lookup: Fast retrieval by tenant ID (no scanning required)
  • Caching support: Includes ETag header for conditional requests
  • Error handling: Returns 404 if tenant doesn't exist

Responses:

  • 200 OK: Tenant found and details returned successfully
  • 401 Unauthorized: Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 403 Forbidden: User lacks required admin:all scope
  • 404 Not Found: No tenant exists with the specified ID

Examples:

# Get a specific tenant by ID
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants/tenant-501a149f" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"

# Get tenant with response headers shown
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants/tenant-abc123" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
     -v

# Example successful response:
# {
#   "id": "tenant-501a149f",
#   "name": "ACME Corporation",
#   "admin_email": "admin@acme.com",
#   "metadata": {"region": "us-east-1", "tier": "premium"},
#   "created_at": "2025-10-11T08:30:00Z",
#   "updated_at": "2025-10-11T08:30:00Z"
# }

admin-tenants.title: Why we need this endpoint:
admin-tenants.descriptionHTML:
PATCH /v1/admin/tenants/{tenant_id} – Modify tenant configuration

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Tenant information changes over time (new admin email, updated metadata)
  • Allows updating specific fields without replacing the entire tenant record
  • Without it, admins would need to delete and recreate tenants (losing history)
  • Essential for maintaining accurate tenant data as organizations evolve

What it does:

  • Updates one or more fields of an existing tenant
  • Only changes the fields you specify (leaves others unchanged)
  • Intelligently merges metadata (adds new keys, updates existing ones)
  • Validates all updates before applying them

Access:

  • Only administrators with admin:all scope can update tenants
  • Requires X-Tenant-Id header for audit trail

Behavior:

  • Partial updates: Send only the fields you want to change
  • Metadata merging: New metadata keys are added; existing keys are updated; set to null to remove
  • Validation: Email format and name length are checked before saving
  • Empty requests rejected: At least one field must be provided

Responses:

  • 200 OK: Tenant successfully updated with new values
  • 400 Bad Request: Empty request body (no fields to update)
  • 401 Unauthorized: Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 403 Forbidden: User lacks required admin:all scope
  • 404 Not Found: Tenant with specified ID doesn't exist
  • 422 Unprocessable Entity: Invalid email format or validation errors

Examples:

# Update tenant name only
curl -X PATCH "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants/tenant-501a149f" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -H "X-Tenant-Id: tenant-admin-root" \
     -d '{
       "name": "ACME Corp (Updated)"
     }'

# Update admin email
curl -X PATCH "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants/tenant-abc123" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{
       "admin_email": "newadmin@acme.com"
     }'

# Update metadata (merges with existing metadata)
curl -X PATCH "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants/tenant-501a149f" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{
       "metadata": {
         "region": "us-west-2",
         "tier": "enterprise",
         "new_field": "value"
       }
     }'

# Update multiple fields at once
curl -X PATCH "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants/tenant-xyz789" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{
       "name": "Updated Name",
       "admin_email": "updated@example.com",
       "metadata": {"status": "active"}
     }'

admin-tenants.title: Why we need this endpoint:
admin-tenants.descriptionHTML:
DELETE /v1/admin/tenants/{tenant_id} – Remove a tenant from the platform

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Organizations may leave the platform and need to be removed
  • Essential for cleanup during testing or when closing customer accounts
  • Without it, deleted/inactive tenants would accumulate in the system
  • Required for compliance with data removal requirements

What it does:

  • Permanently removes a tenant and its configuration from the platform
  • Checks for dependent resources before deletion (safe deletion policy)
  • Prevents accidental data loss by blocking deletion of active tenants
  • Records deletion event in audit logs for compliance

Access:

  • Only administrators with admin:all scope can delete tenants
  • Requires X-Tenant-Id header for audit trail

Behavior:

  • Dependency checking: Fails if tenant has active providers, jobs, or other resources
  • Safe deletion: Won't delete until all dependencies are removed first
  • Not idempotent: Deleting non-existent tenant returns 404 (explicit failure)
  • No response body: Returns 204 with empty body on success

Responses:

  • 204 No Content: Tenant successfully deleted (empty response body)
  • 401 Unauthorized: Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 403 Forbidden: User lacks required admin:all scope
  • 404 Not Found: Tenant with specified ID doesn't exist
  • 409 Conflict: Cannot delete tenant because it has active resources (providers, jobs, etc.)

Examples:

# Delete a tenant (succeeds only if no dependencies)
curl -X DELETE "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants/tenant-501a149f" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
     -H "X-Tenant-Id: tenant-admin-root"

# Delete tenant with verbose output to see headers
curl -X DELETE "http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/tenants/tenant-xyz789" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
     -v

# Example 409 response (tenant has dependencies):
# {
#   "type": "https://example.com/probs/conflict",
#   "title": "Conflict",
#   "status": 409,
#   "detail": "Cannot delete tenant with dependent resources",
#   "instance": "/v1/admin/tenants/tenant-501a149f",
#   "extensions": {
#     "blockers": [
#       {"type": "provider", "id": "provider-abc", "name": "OpenAI GPT-4"},
#       {"type": "job", "id": "job-xyz", "status": "running"}
#     ]
#   }
# }
#
# To delete this tenant: first remove/delete the providers and jobs listed

models-providers.title: RBAC
models-providers.descriptionHTML:
List configured runtime LLM providers (registry-only, Redis-backed).

RBAC: Requires admin:all scope. Returns providers exactly as previously registered via POST /v1/admin/models/providers/register. No discovery logic.

Multi-tenant visibility:

  • Admin users see all providers (global + all tenant-scoped)
  • Providers with tenant_id=null are global (available to all tenants)
  • Providers with specific tenant_id are scoped to that tenant only
  • Future non-admin endpoint would filter to user's tenant + global providers

Pagination:

  • Query params: page_size (integer, 1-1000, default 100), page_token (string, optional)
  • Returns: {items: Provider[], next_page_token?: string, total?: number}
  • Link header (RFC 5988) included when next page available

Caching:

  • Supports If-None-Match header for conditional requests
  • Returns 304 Not Modified if ETag matches
  • ETag header always present on 200 responses

Response headers:

  • ETag: Content hash for caching
  • Link: Next page URL (when applicable)
  • X-Request-Id: Request correlation ID
  • RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset: Rate limit status

Provider config:

  • config field may contain arbitrary provider-specific keys added via PATCH
  • Schema accepts extra fields to support custom provider configurations
  • Nested objects are preserved (e.g., config.custom_field.nested_value)

Secret redaction:

  • api_key: Always null or masked ("***")
  • has_api_key: Boolean indicating if api_key is configured
  • config.headers.authorization, config.auth.token: Masked

models-providers.title: RBAC
models-providers.descriptionHTML:
Register a new runtime LLM provider with the platform.

Admin-only operation to add or register an external LLM endpoint for use by the orchestrator. The request should include the provider name, base_url, and optional fields like model and api_key. On success the provider will be available for selection and orchestration.

RBAC: Requires admin:all scope.

Tenant scoping:

  • tenant_id (optional): If provided, provider is scoped to that tenant only
  • If omitted or null: Provider is global and available to all tenants
  • Admin users see all providers (global + tenant-scoped) in LIST
  • Future non-admin endpoints would filter by user's tenant

Request validation:

  • name: Required, 1-255 characters
  • type: Required, must be openai_compatible or custom
  • base_url: Required for openai_compatible type
  • api_key: Optional, will be stored securely and never returned in responses

Idempotency:

  • Registering same (tenant_id, name) with identical config → 200 OK (no-op, idempotent)
  • Comparison normalizes configs (ignores key order, compares api_key presence via has_api_key boolean)
  • Registering same name with different config → 409 Conflict with diff details in X-Conflict-Details header

Status codes:

  • 200: Provider registered successfully (or idempotent no-op)
  • 400: Business logic error (e.g., egress not allowed)
  • 403: Forbidden (egress allowlist violation)
  • 409: Conflict (provider exists with different config)
  • 422: Validation error (invalid fields)

models-providers.title: RBAC
models-providers.descriptionHTML:
Get the resolved main LLM provider for a tenant or the global default.

RBAC: Admin-only endpoint (requires admin:all scope).

Resolution precedence:

  1. Tenant-scoped default (if tenant_id provided and tenant has a default)
  2. Global default (if no tenant default exists)
  3. 404 Not Found (if no defaults configured)

Caching:

  • Supports If-None-Match header for conditional requests
  • Returns 304 Not Modified if ETag matches
  • ETag header always present on 200 responses

Status codes:

  • 200: Default provider found and returned
  • 304: Not Modified (ETag match)
  • 404: No default provider configured

models-providers.title: RBAC
models-providers.descriptionHTML:
Retrieve detailed information about a specific runtime LLM provider.

RBAC: Admin-only endpoint (requires admin:all scope).

Secret redaction:

  • api_key: Always null or masked
  • has_api_key: Boolean indicator showing if api_key is configured
  • config.headers.authorization, config.auth.token: Masked

Caching:

  • Supports If-None-Match header for conditional requests
  • Returns 304 Not Modified if ETag matches
  • ETag header always present on 200 responses

Status codes:

  • 200: Provider found and returned
  • 304: Not Modified (ETag match)
  • 404: Provider not found

Response headers:

  • ETag: Content hash for caching
  • X-Request-Id: Request correlation ID

models-providers.title: RBAC
models-providers.descriptionHTML:
Update registration details for an existing runtime LLM provider.

RBAC: Admin-only operation (requires admin:all scope).

Behavior:

  • Supply any optional fields (base_url, model, api_key, tenant_id, config) to update
  • Config fields are merged (not replaced) - provide partial updates
  • Arbitrary config keys are supported (provider-specific customization)
  • Provider is re-validated after merge
  • Orchestrator is notified of changes

Flexible config:

  • You can add arbitrary provider-specific keys under config
  • Nested objects are preserved (e.g., config.custom_field.nested_value)
  • LIST endpoint will return all config keys without validation errors
  • Redaction rules still apply: api_key, auth.token, headers.authorization are masked

Status codes:

  • 200: Provider updated successfully (includes trace_id/event_id)
  • 400: Empty body (at least one field required)
  • 403: Forbidden (egress allowlist violation)
  • 404: Provider not found
  • 422: Validation error (invalid merged config)

Response: ActionResponse with trace_id and event_id for auditing

models-providers.title: RBAC
models-providers.descriptionHTML:
Unregister and remove a runtime LLM provider from the platform.

RBAC: Admin-only operation (requires admin:all scope).

Behavior:

  • Completely removes provider from registry
  • Auto-clears all defaults: If provider is set as default (global or tenant), it is automatically cleared before deletion
  • Orchestrator is notified of removal
  • Safe deletion: No errors if provider was set as default

Auto-clear defaults policy:

  • Checks all default scopes (global + all tenants)
  • Clears any defaults pointing to this provider
  • Clears both in-memory and Redis cache keys
  • Atomic operation: defaults cleared, then provider deleted

Status codes:

  • 204: Provider successfully deleted (no response body, but includes headers)
  • 404: Provider not found

Response headers (always present on 204):

  • X-Request-Id: Request correlation ID
  • X-Event-Id: Event/provenance ID for auditing
  • X-Trace-Id: Distributed trace ID

models-providers.title: RBAC
models-providers.descriptionHTML:
Set a runtime LLM provider as the global or tenant-scoped default.

RBAC: Admin-only endpoint (requires admin:all scope).

Behavior:

  • If tenant_id is not provided or null: Sets global default provider
  • If tenant_id is provided: Sets tenant-scoped default provider
  • Provider must exist or 404 is returned

Default resolution precedence (for context):

  1. Tenant-scoped default (if request has tenant and tenant has default)
  2. Global default (if no tenant default)
  3. 404 (if no defaults configured)

Status codes:

  • 200: Default provider successfully set (includes trace_id/event_id)
  • 404: Provider not found
  • 400: Business logic error

Response: ActionResponse with trace_id and event_id for auditing

models-instances.title: GET /instances
models-instances.descriptionHTML:
GET /instances – View all available AI models

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Users and admins need to discover which AI models are available to use
  • Applications need to show users a catalog of models they can interact with
  • Without this, users wouldn't know which models exist or how to reference them in API calls

What it does:

  • Returns a paginated list of all registered AI model instances
  • Shows key details: model name, provider, capabilities, loaded status, and availability
  • Non-admin users only see enabled models; admins can see all models including disabled ones

Access:

  • Any authenticated user with user:me permission
  • Admins with admin:all have additional visibility into disabled models

Behavior:

  • Supports HTTP caching via ETag (returns 304 Not Modified when content hasn't changed)
  • Pagination: Use page_size (1-1000, default 100) and page_token for large result sets
  • Filtering: Filter by tenant_id, provider_id, loaded, or enabled status
  • Non-admin users automatically get enabled=true filter (only see active models)
  • Admin users can override filters to see disabled or unloaded models

Responses:

  • 200 OK – Returns list of model instances with pagination metadata
  • 304 Not Modified – No changes since last request (use If-None-Match header with ETag)
  • 401 Unauthorized – Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 403 Forbidden – User lacks required permissions

Examples:

# List all available models (user view - enabled only)
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/instances" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN"

# Admin: List all models including disabled ones
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/instances?enabled=false" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"

# Filter by provider and use pagination
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/instances?provider_id=ollama-local&page_size=50" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN"

# Use caching (304 if unchanged)
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/instances" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" \
  -H 'If-None-Match: "abc123def456"'

models-instances.title: POST /instances
models-instances.descriptionHTML:
POST /instances – Register a new AI model instance (Admin only)

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Platform admins need to add new AI models to the system as they become available
  • Allows connecting to new model providers (OpenAI, Ollama, Azure, etc.) and specific model versions
  • Without this, the platform would be limited to whatever models were pre-configured at deployment

What it does:

  • Registers a new model instance in PostgreSQL with configuration details
  • Marks the model as loaded=true and makes it available for use
  • Records the model's capabilities (chat, embeddings, etc.) and provider information
  • Invalidates the instance list cache to reflect the new model immediately

Access:

  • Admin only – Requires admin:all permission
  • Regular users with user:me permission will receive 403 Forbidden

Behavior:

  • Idempotent: Use the Idempotency-Key header to prevent duplicate creates
    • If replayed within 24 hours, returns 200 OK with existing instance (not 201 Created)
    • Without the key, duplicate POSTs create multiple instances with the same name
  • Creates audit log entry for compliance tracking
  • Automatically sets loaded=true on creation

Responses:

  • 201 Created – Model instance successfully registered (first time)
  • 200 OK – Idempotent replay detected, returning existing instance
  • 400 Bad Request – Invalid request data (missing fields, invalid provider_id, etc.)
  • 401 Unauthorized – Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 403 Forbidden – User is not an admin
  • 409 Conflict – Instance with same name already exists in tenant (without idempotency key)

Examples:

# Create a new Ollama model instance
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/instances" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: create-llama-3.2-$(date +%s)" \
  -d '{
    "name": "llama-3.2-3b",
    "provider_id": "ollama-local",
    "model_id": "llama3.2:3b-instruct",
    "tenant_id": null,
    "enabled": true,
    "capabilities": ["chat"]
  }'

# Create an OpenAI GPT-4 instance for a specific tenant
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/instances" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "gpt-4-turbo",
    "provider_id": "openai-azure",
    "model_id": "gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09",
    "tenant_id": "tenant-123",
    "enabled": true,
    "capabilities": ["chat", "vision"]
  }'

models-instances.title: GET /defaults
models-instances.descriptionHTML:
GET /defaults – Get your default AI model (with smart fallback)

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Applications need to know which model to use when the user doesn't specify one
  • Users can have personal preferences, while organizations can set company-wide defaults
  • Without this, every API call would require explicitly choosing a model, creating poor UX

What it does:

  • Returns the default model for the current user with automatic precedence resolution
  • Checks user's personal preference first, then organization default, then global system default
  • Tells you which level was used via the X-Default-Scope header (user, tenant, or global)

Access:

  • Any authenticated user with user:me permission
  • Admins with admin:all can also access this endpoint

Behavior:

  • Precedence Order (highest to lowest):
    1. User default – Your personal preference (specific to your user ID + organization)
    2. Tenant default – Your organization's company-wide default
    3. Global default – System-wide fallback (when no user/tenant default is set)
  • HTTP Caching: Returns ETag header for efficient caching
    • Send If-None-Match: "<etag>" to get 304 Not Modified when unchanged
    • ETag changes when the default model changes or when the scope changes
    • 304 responses have no body – use your cached version
  • Tenant Override: Send X-Tenant-Id header to check a specific organization's defaults
  • Vary Header: Response includes Vary: Authorization, X-Tenant-Id for correct cache behavior

Responses:

  • 200 OK – Default model found and returned (includes X-Default-Scope header)
  • 304 Not Modified – Content unchanged since last request (use cached version)
  • 404 Not Found – No default model configured at any level (set one via PATCH /defaults)
  • 401 Unauthorized – Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 403 Forbidden – User lacks required permissions

Examples:

# Get your current default model
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/defaults" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN"

# Response (200 OK):
# Headers:
#   X-Default-Scope: user
#   ETag: "43902c7efe456853"
#   Vary: Authorization, X-Tenant-Id
# Body:
# {
#   "chat": {
#     "instance_id": "6491b020-bbe3-47fe-991e-e7c21a15260c",
#     "name": "llama-3.2-3b",
#     "provider_id": "ollama-local",
#     "model_id": "llama3.2:3b-instruct"
#   },
#   "etag": "43902c7efe456853"
# }

# Use caching to save bandwidth (304 if unchanged)
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/defaults" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" \
  -H 'If-None-Match: "43902c7efe456853"'

# Response (304 Not Modified):
# Headers:
#   X-Default-Scope: user
#   ETag: "43902c7efe456853"
# Body: (empty - use cached version)

# Check a specific tenant's defaults (requires tenant access)
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/defaults" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" \
  -H "X-Tenant-Id: tenant-123"

models-instances.title: PATCH /defaults
models-instances.descriptionHTML:
PATCH /defaults – Set your default AI model (or organization/global defaults)

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Users need a way to set their personal default model preference
  • Admins need to set organization-wide defaults for all team members
  • Platform operators need to set global fallback defaults for all users
  • Without this, users would have to specify a model on every single API call

What it does:

  • Sets the default model at one of three scope levels: user (personal), tenant (organization), or global (system-wide)
  • Validates that the model instance exists and is enabled before setting it
  • Invalidates cached defaults so the change takes effect immediately

Access:

  • User scope: Any authenticated user with user:me can set their personal default
  • Tenant scope: Admins with admin:all can set organization-wide defaults
  • Global scope: Admins with admin:all can set system-wide fallback defaults

Behavior:

  • Scope Selection: Use the X-Default-Scope header to choose scope level:
    • user (default) – Your personal preference (user ID + tenant ID)
    • tenant – Organization-wide default for all users in your tenant (admin only)
    • global – System-wide fallback for all users (admin only)
  • Tenant ID: For tenant scope, send X-Tenant-Id header with the tenant identifier
  • Validation: Checks that the instance exists and is enabled (disabled instances return 409 Conflict)
  • Cache Invalidation: ETag changes immediately after update (GET /defaults reflects new default)
  • Multiple Formats Supported:
    • Preferred: {"chat": {"instance_id": "<uuid>"}} (fastest, no lookup)
    • Legacy: {"chat": {"name": "<instance-name>"}} (requires database lookup)
    • Deprecated: {"name": "<instance-name>"} (top-level, use chat.instance_id instead)

Responses:

  • 200 OK – Default model updated successfully (returns instance details and confirmed scope)
  • 400 Bad Request – Invalid scope, missing headers, or semantic errors
  • 401 Unauthorized – Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 403 Forbidden – User lacks permissions for requested scope (e.g., non-admin trying tenant/global)
  • 404 Not Found – Instance not found by ID or name
  • 409 Conflict – Instance exists but is disabled (cannot set disabled models as defaults)
  • 422 Unprocessable Entity – Schema validation errors (unknown fields, missing required fields)

Examples:

# Set your personal default (user scope)
curl -X PATCH "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/defaults" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"chat": {"instance_id": "6491b020-bbe3-47fe-991e-e7c21a15260c"}}'

# Response (200 OK):
# {
#   "chat": {
#     "instance_id": "6491b020-bbe3-47fe-991e-e7c21a15260c",
#     "instance_name": "llama-3.2-3b",
#     "provider_id": "ollama-local",
#     "model_id": "llama3.2:3b-instruct"
#   },
#   "scope": "user"
# }

# Admin: Set organization-wide default (tenant scope)
curl -X PATCH "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/defaults" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Default-Scope: tenant" \
  -H "X-Tenant-Id: tenant-123" \
  -d '{"chat": {"instance_id": "abc-def-ghi"}}'

# Admin: Set global system fallback (global scope)
curl -X PATCH "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/defaults" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Default-Scope: global" \
  -d '{"chat": {"instance_id": "xyz-123-456"}}'

# Legacy format: Set default by instance name (requires lookup)
curl -X PATCH "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/defaults" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"chat": {"name": "llama-3.2-3b"}}'

# Error example: Non-admin trying to set tenant default (403 Forbidden)
curl -X PATCH "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/defaults" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" \
  -H "X-Default-Scope: tenant" \
  -d '{"chat": {"instance_id": "..."}}'
# Response: {"detail": "Permission denied: tenant scope requires admin privileges"}

IMPORTANT: Send the raw JSON from the examples above. DO NOT wrap in summary/description/value fields.

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Applications need detailed model specifications before making API calls
  • Users want to know a model's capabilities (chat, vision, embeddings, etc.) and configuration
  • Developers need to inspect model parameters, context window sizes, and provider settings
  • Without this, users would have to guess model capabilities or maintain separate documentation

What it does:

  • Returns complete details for a single model instance by its UUID
  • Shows capabilities, parameters, modalities, provider info, tenant scope, and enabled status
  • Includes metadata like creation time, loaded status, and configuration settings

Access:

    • Send If-None-Match: "<etag>" to get 304 Not Modified when unchanged
    • 304 responses have no body – use your cached version
  • Non-admin users: Can only see enabled instances
  • Admin users: Can see all instances including disabled ones

Responses:

  • 200 OK – Instance details retrieved successfully (includes ETag header)
  • 304 Not Modified – Content unchanged since last request (use cached version)
  • 401 Unauthorized – Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 403 Forbidden – User lacks required permissions
  • 404 Not Found – Instance does not exist with given UUID

models-instances.title: DELETE /instances/{instance_id}
models-instances.descriptionHTML:
DELETE /instances/{instance_id} – Remove an AI model from the platform (Admin only)

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Admins need to decommission outdated or unused model instances
  • Platform operators need to clean up test models or free resources
  • Organizations need to remove models that are no longer needed or supported
  • Without this, unused models would accumulate indefinitely, cluttering the instance list

What it does:

  • Marks the model instance as unloaded or fully removes it from the database
  • Acquires an exclusive lock to prevent concurrent operations (race condition protection)
  • Invalidates all related caches (instance list, defaults) to reflect the deletion immediately
  • Returns 204 No Content on successful deletion (empty response body)

Access:

  • Admin only – Requires admin:all permission
  • Regular users with user:me permission will receive 403 Forbidden

Behavior:

  • Idempotent: Deleting an already-deleted instance returns 404 Not Found (not an error state)
  • Locking: Acquires exclusive lock during deletion to prevent race conditions
  • Cache Invalidation: Clears instance list cache and any defaults that referenced this instance
  • Audit Trail: Records deletion event in audit log for compliance tracking

Responses:

  • 204 No Content – Instance successfully deleted (empty response body)
  • 401 Unauthorized – Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 403 Forbidden – User is not an admin
  • 404 Not Found – Instance does not exist with given UUID (already deleted or never existed)
  • 500 Internal Server Error – Unexpected server-side error during deletion

Examples:

# Admin: Delete a model instance
curl -X DELETE "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/instances/6491b020-bbe3-47fe-991e-e7c21a15260c" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"

# Response (204 No Content):
# Headers:
#   (no special headers)
# Body: (empty)

# Error example: Non-admin user trying to delete (403 Forbidden)
curl -X DELETE "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/instances/6491b020-bbe3-47fe-991e-e7c21a15260c" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN"
# Response: {"type": "about:blank", "title": "Forbidden", "status": 403, ...}

# Error example: Instance does not exist (404 Not Found)
curl -X DELETE "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/instances/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"
# Response: {"type": "about:blank", "title": "Not Found", "status": 404, ...}

# Idempotent: Deleting the same instance twice returns 404 on second attempt
curl -X DELETE "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/instances/abc-123-def" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"
# First call: 204 No Content
# Second call: 404 Not Found

models-instances.title: POST /instances/{instance_id}/tests
models-instances.descriptionHTML:
POST /instances/{instance_id}/tests – Send a test prompt to an AI model

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Users need to verify that a model works before integrating it into their application
  • Developers want to test model behavior with different prompts and parameters
  • Teams need to compare model outputs side-by-side to choose the best one
  • Without this, users would have to build a full integration just to see if a model works

What it does:

  • Sends a chat completion request to the model provider using the instance's configuration
  • Returns the generated text along with observability metadata (provider, latency, parameters used)
  • Validates that the instance exists, is enabled, and is loaded before sending the request
  • Provides a quick "smoke test" to confirm connectivity and basic functionality

Access:

  • Any authenticated user with user:me permission
  • Admins with admin:all can also access this endpoint
  • Users can only test enabled model instances

Behavior:

  • Default Parameters: Uses sensible defaults if not specified:
    • temperature=0.0 (deterministic output for testing)
    • max_tokens=64 (short response to avoid long waits)
    • `stop=["

", "```", "---"]` (stop at natural boundaries)

  • Timeout: 60-second read timeout to accommodate slower models
  • Demo Mode: Returns "pong" response for "ping" prompt when no providers are registered (testing mode)
  • Observability: Response includes provider ID, latency, token count, and parameters used
  • Non-admin users: Can only test enabled instances (disabled instances return 403 Forbidden)

Responses:

  • 200 OK – Test completed successfully (returns generated text and metadata)
  • 400 Bad Request – Invalid request (missing prompt, invalid parameters, etc.)
  • 401 Unauthorized – Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 403 Forbidden – User lacks permissions or instance is disabled
  • 404 Not Found – Instance does not exist with given UUID
  • 500 Internal Server Error – Provider error or unexpected server-side failure

Examples:

# Test a model with a simple factual question (deterministic)
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/v1/models/instances/6491b020-bbe3-47fe-991e-e7c21a15260c/tests" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \

  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_TOKEN" \

tools.title: GET /tools – Discover available tools
tools.descriptionHTML:
GET /tools – Discover available tools

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Tool discovery: AI agents and client apps need to know what tools are available before they can invoke them.
  • Dynamic capabilities: Tools can be added or removed at runtime, so clients must query to see the current set.
  • Permission awareness: Shows only tools the current user has permission to use, preventing unauthorized access attempts.
  • Schema introspection: Returns input schemas so clients can construct valid tool invocation requests.
  • Without this endpoint, clients would have to hardcode tool names and wouldn't know about new tools or permission changes.

What it does:

  • Scans the src.mcp.tools package and returns a best-effort list of detected tools.
  • Shows which tools are invokable vs. namespaces (non-invokable groupings).
  • Provides metadata: name, entrypoint, input schema, required permissions, and capabilities.
  • Returns up to 50 tools per page with has_more indicating if additional items exist.

Access:

  • Requires tools:basic, tools:all, or admin:all scope.
  • Visibility follows RBAC rules: admin-only tools hidden from non-admins, basic tools visible to tools:basic holders.

Behavior:

  • Filtering: By default only invokable tools are returned (namespaces excluded).
  • Caching: Supports conditional GET via If-None-Match/ETag (304 on cache hit).
  • Headers: Sets Cache-Control: private, max-age=30 and Vary: Authorization.
  • Redaction: Non-admin callers see redacted module paths (null instead of internal paths).

Responses:

  • 200 OK: Returns ToolsListResponse with items array, total count, and pagination flags.
  • 304 Not Modified: When If-None-Match matches current ETag (no changes).
  • 401 Unauthorized: Missing or invalid auth token.
  • 500 Internal Server Error: Unexpected failure during tool discovery.

Examples:

# List all available tools
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN' \
  https://api.example.com/v1/tools

# Conditional GET (check for updates)
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN' \
  -H 'If-None-Match: W/"abc123"' \
  https://api.example.com/v1/tools
# → 304 if unchanged

tools.title: POST /tools/{name}/invocations – Execute a tool and get results
tools.descriptionHTML:
POST /tools/{name}/invocations – Execute a tool and get results

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Tool execution: AI agents and automated workflows need to run tools to accomplish tasks (querying databases, processing data, etc.).
  • Result retrieval: Returns structured output that agents can parse and use for decision-making.
  • Idempotent retries: Network failures are common; idempotency keys prevent duplicate executions when retrying failed requests.
  • Audit trail: Creates permanent invocation records with timing and provenance for compliance and debugging.
  • Without this endpoint, agents would need direct database access or custom code for each operation, creating security risks and maintenance burden.

What it does:

  • Invokes the named tool (e.g., graph.query) with provided arguments.
  • Returns structured results with provenance tracking (trace_id/event_id) and timing.
  • Creates a retrievable invocation record at /v1/tools/{name}/invocations/{event_id}.
  • Supports idempotent execution via Idempotency-Key header (replay returns 200 instead of 201).

Access:

  • Requires tools:basic, tools:all, or admin:all scope.
  • Per-tool RBAC enforced: some tools require elevated permissions beyond route-level auth.

Behavior:

  • Request body: ToolInvokeRequest with args (JSON object → kwargs) and optional timeout_seconds (1-3600).
  • Idempotency: Supply Idempotency-Key header to cache results for 24h; replays return 200 OK with Idempotency-Replayed: true.
  • Validation: Pre-invocation JSON Schema validation when tool exposes INPUT_SCHEMA.
  • Headers: Returns Location header pointing to invocation resource, X-Request-Id with event_id.

Responses:

  • 201 Created: New invocation executed successfully (includes Location header).
  • 200 OK: Idempotent replay of previous invocation (includes Idempotency-Replayed: true).
  • 400 Bad Request: Invalid arguments (failed schema validation).
  • 401 Unauthorized: Missing or invalid auth token.
  • 403 Forbidden: Caller lacks required permission for this specific tool.
  • 404 Not Found: Tool doesn't exist or is non-invokable (namespace).
  • 500 Internal Server Error: Tool execution failed.

Examples:

# Invoke graph.query tool
curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"args": {"cypher": "MATCH (n) RETURN count(n)"}}' \
  https://api.example.com/v1/tools/graph.query/invocations

# Idempotent invocation (safe retry)
curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN' \
  -H 'Idempotency-Key: my-unique-key-123' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"args": {"query": "test"}}' \
  https://api.example.com/v1/tools/system.health/invocations
# → 201 first time, 200 on replay

# Invoke with timeout
curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"args": {"operation": "long"}, "timeout_seconds": 30}' \
  https://api.example.com/v1/tools/data.process/invocations

tools.title: GET /tools/{name}/invocations/{eid} – Retrieve stored invocation result
tools.descriptionHTML:
GET /tools/{name}/invocations/{eid} – Retrieve stored invocation result

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Asynchronous workflows: Agents can retrieve results later instead of waiting for long-running tools to complete.
  • Audit and compliance: Permanently stored invocation records provide an audit trail showing who did what and when.
  • Debugging assistance: When tool invocations fail, developers can inspect the exact inputs, outputs, and errors.
  • Result sharing: Team members can reference specific invocation IDs when discussing issues or outcomes.
  • Without this endpoint, results would be lost after initial retrieval, making debugging and auditing impossible.

What it does:

  • Returns the exact stored result for a specific tool invocation (by event_id).
  • Provides access to historical invocation data for auditing, debugging, or result retrieval.
  • Enforces anti-enumeration: only the invocation owner or admins can access (non-owners get 404).

Access:

  • Requires valid auth token (any authenticated user can attempt access).
  • Owner-only: Only the user who created the invocation (by token sub) or admins can fetch.
  • Anti-enumeration: Non-owners receive 404 (not 403) to prevent invocation ID discovery.

Behavior:

  • Path validation: name must match the tool that produced eid; mismatches return 404.
  • UUID validation: eid must be a valid UUID; invalid formats return 400.
  • Retention: Results retained per RETENTION_DAYS setting; expired invocations return 404.
  • Caching: Supports If-None-Match/ETag for 304 responses; sets Cache-Control: private, max-age=30.
  • Headers: Returns X-Request-Id: {eid} and Vary: Authorization.

Responses:

  • 200 OK: Successfully retrieved invocation result (returns ToolInvokeResponse).
  • 304 Not Modified: If-None-Match matches current ETag (no changes).
  • 400 Bad Request: Invalid eid format (not a UUID).
  • 401 Unauthorized: Missing or invalid auth token.
  • 404 Not Found: Unknown invocation, expired, name mismatch, or caller not authorized (anti-enumeration).

Examples:

# Retrieve invocation result
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN' \
  https://api.example.com/v1/tools/graph.query/invocations/33200c38-7bb0-47ea-9765-763c78315841

# Conditional GET (check for updates)
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN' \
  -H 'If-None-Match: W/"def456"' \
  https://api.example.com/v1/tools/graph.query/invocations/33200c38-7bb0-47ea-9765-763c78315841
# → 304 if unchanged

# Non-owner attempt (anti-enumeration)
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer OTHER_USER_TOKEN' \
  https://api.example.com/v1/tools/system.health/invocations/abc-def-ghi
# → 404 (not 403, to prevent ID discovery)

tools.title: GET /tools/{name} – Fetch metadata for a specific tool
tools.descriptionHTML:
GET /tools/{name} – Fetch metadata for a specific tool

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Input validation: Client apps need the JSON schema to validate user inputs before submitting expensive or risky operations.
  • Dynamic UI generation: Front-end frameworks can render appropriate form fields based on the schema (text inputs, dropdowns, etc.).
  • Documentation discovery: Developers inspecting a tool can see exactly what parameters it accepts and what they mean.
  • Permission checking: Shows whether a tool requires elevated permissions before attempting to invoke it.
  • Without this endpoint, clients would have to hardcode validation rules or submit invalid requests, wasting API calls and user time.

What it does:

  • Returns detailed metadata about a single tool: module path, entrypoint, description, input schema.
  • Helps client UIs render tool-specific forms or validate arguments before invocation.
  • Provides schema for input validation (JSON Schema format when available).

Access:

  • Requires tools:basic, tools:all, or admin:all scope.
  • Visibility rules: Admin-only tools hidden from non-admins (404 instead of 403 for anti-enumeration).
  • Redaction: Non-admin callers see redacted module paths (null instead of internal paths).

Behavior:

  • Schema detection: Checks INPUT_SCHEMA, get_input_schema(), or describe() methods.
  • Namespace handling: Returns 404 for namespaces (non-invokable groupings).
  • Caching: Supports If-None-Match/ETag for 304 responses; sets Cache-Control: private, max-age=30.
  • Headers: Returns Vary: Authorization to vary by user permissions.

Responses:

  • 200 OK: Successfully retrieved tool metadata (returns ToolInfo).
  • 304 Not Modified: If-None-Match matches current ETag (no changes).
  • 401 Unauthorized: Missing or invalid auth token.
  • 404 Not Found: Unknown tool, namespace, or not visible to caller's scopes (anti-enumeration).

Examples:

# Get metadata for graph.query tool
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN' \
  https://api.example.com/v1/tools/graph.query

# Conditional GET (check for schema updates)
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN' \
  -H 'If-None-Match: W/"xyz789"' \
  https://api.example.com/v1/tools/system.health
# → 304 if unchanged

# Attempt to access admin-only tool (non-admin caller)
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer USER_TOKEN' \
  https://api.example.com/v1/tools/security.audit
# → 404 (anti-enumeration, not 403)

jobs.title: Why we need this endpoint:
jobs.descriptionHTML:
GET /v1/jobs – List your background jobs

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Progress monitoring: Users need to see which of their long-running operations are still processing vs. complete.
  • Error discovery: Shows which jobs failed so users can investigate and retry.
  • Job management: Users can find job IDs to cancel unwanted operations or retrieve results.
  • Dashboard building: Front-end apps display job lists to give users visibility into background work.
  • Without this endpoint, users wouldn't know if their requests succeeded, failed, or are still running.

What it does:

  • Returns all jobs you created, with optional filtering by status
  • Supports pagination for large result sets
  • Includes caching to reduce server load when polling

Access:

  • Any authenticated user (shows only your own jobs)
  • Admin users should use /admin/jobs to see all users' jobs

Behavior:

  • Filtering: Add ?status=running or ?status=queued&status=running to filter results
  • Pagination: Results are sorted newest first (default 25 per page, max 50). Use next_page_token from response to get more
  • Caching: Returns ETag header. Send it back as If-None-Match to get 304 Not Modified when nothing changed
  • Privacy: You only see your own jobs (filtered by token owner). Other users' jobs return empty list

Responses:

  • 200: OK – Job list with pagination info (items, total, has_more, next_page_token)
  • 304: Not Modified – No changes since your last request (when using If-None-Match)
  • 400: Bad Request – Invalid page_token (must be numeric offset like '0', '25')
  • 401: Unauthorized – Missing or invalid authentication token

Examples:

# List all your jobs
curl -X GET http://localhost:8000/v1/jobs \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

# Filter by status
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/v1/jobs?status=running&status=queued" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

# Efficient polling with ETag (returns 304 if unchanged)
curl -X GET http://localhost:8000/v1/jobs \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -H "If-None-Match: W/\"abc123\""

jobs.title: Why we need this endpoint:
jobs.descriptionHTML:
POST /v1/jobs – Submit a new background job

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Async operations: Long-running tasks shouldn't block API requests; this endpoint queues work and returns immediately.
  • Scalability: Background jobs can be processed by separate worker services, allowing the API to remain responsive.
  • Retry safety: With idempotency keys, clients can safely retry failed requests without creating duplicate jobs.
  • Job tracking: Returns job ID so clients can monitor progress, retrieve results, or cancel if needed.
  • Without this endpoint, all operations would be synchronous, causing timeouts and blocking other users' requests.

What it does:

  • Creates a new background job and returns immediately (doesn't wait for completion)
  • Returns job ID and status URL so you can poll or stream progress
  • Automatically deduplicates identical requests (idempotency)

Access:

  • Any authenticated user can create jobs
  • Job owner is automatically set to your token subject (sub claim)
  • No admin permission required

Behavior:

  • Idempotency: Send Idempotency-Key header to prevent duplicate jobs. Same key within 24h returns existing job (200 OK) instead of creating new one (202 Accepted)
  • Auto-deduplication: Even without explicit key, identical payload from same user is deduplicated
  • Job types: Must be in allowed list (e.g., 'demo', 'test'). Check API config for valid types
  • Retention: Jobs auto-expire after creation (Redis: 10 days TTL, Memory: 7 days background sweep)
  • Backend: Configure via JOB_STORE_BACKEND env (memory or redis)

Responses:

  • 202: Accepted – New job created successfully. Returns {"id": "...", "status": "queued", "owner": "you@example.com"}
  • 200: OK – Idempotent replay (same request already processed). Returns existing job with Idempotency-Replayed: true header
  • 400: Bad Request – Unknown job type or invalid payload schema
  • 401: Unauthorized – Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 422: Validation Error – Malformed request body

Examples:

# Create a new job
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/jobs \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"type": "demo", "payload": {"duration_ms": 2000}}'

# Create with idempotency key (safe retry)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/jobs \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -H "Idempotency-Key: my-unique-key-123" \
     -d '{"type": "demo", "payload": {"duration_ms": 2000}}'

jobs.title: Why we need this endpoint:
jobs.descriptionHTML:
GET /v1/jobs/{job_id} – Check a specific job's status and result

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Progress checking: After creating a job, users need to check if it completed, failed, or is still running.
  • Result retrieval: Final output data is only available through this endpoint after job completion.
  • Efficient polling: ETag support prevents unnecessary data transfer when job status hasn't changed.
  • Error investigation: Shows failure details and error messages for troubleshooting.
  • Without this endpoint, users would have no way to access job results or know when operations completed.

What it does:

  • Returns the current status of a background job (queued, running, finished, failed, cancelled)
  • Includes the job result when complete
  • Supports efficient polling with conditional requests (ETag/304)

Access:

  • Job owner (the user who created it) can always view
  • Admin users with admin:all permission can view any job
  • Other users get 404 Not Found (anti-enumeration: can't tell if job exists)

Behavior:

  • Caching: Returns ETag header based on job state. Use If-None-Match to get 304 when unchanged
  • Privacy: Non-owners get 404 instead of 403 to prevent job ID guessing
  • Polling: Recommended to poll every 1-2 seconds with ETag, or use SSE endpoint for real-time updates

Responses:

  • 200: OK – Job details (id, status, type, owner, created_at, updated_at, result)
  • 304: Not Modified – Job hasn't changed since your last request (use cached data)
  • 400: Bad Request – Invalid job_id format (must be UUID)
  • 401: Unauthorized – Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 404: Not Found – Job doesn't exist, or you don't have permission to view it

Examples:

# Get job status
curl -X GET http://localhost:8000/v1/jobs/123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000 \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

# Efficient polling with ETag
curl -X GET http://localhost:8000/v1/jobs/123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000 \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -H "If-None-Match: W/\"abc123\"" \
     -i  # Returns 304 if unchanged

jobs.title: Why we need this endpoint:
jobs.descriptionHTML:
DELETE /v1/jobs/{job_id} – Cancel a running or queued job

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Resource cleanup: Stop unnecessary work and free up worker capacity for other jobs.
  • User control: Users need ability to abort jobs that were started by mistake or are no longer needed.
  • Cost savings: Cancelling long-running operations prevents wasted compute time and API costs.
  • Retry safety: Idempotent design means clients can safely retry cancellation without errors.
  • Without this endpoint, users would have no way to stop jobs, wasting resources on unwanted operations.

What it does:

  • Cancels a background job that's queued or running
  • First successful cancel returns 202 Accepted, subsequent calls return 200 OK
  • Safe to retry (idempotent) – won't cause errors if already cancelled or finished

Access:

  • Job owner can cancel their own jobs
  • Admin users with admin:all permission can cancel any job
  • Other users get 404 Not Found (anti-enumeration)

Behavior:

  • Idempotency: First cancel returns 202, all subsequent calls return 200 (safe to retry)
  • Terminal states: Already finished/failed/cancelled jobs return 200 with current status
  • Atomicity: Redis backend uses atomic Lua script for race-free cancellation
  • Privacy: Non-owners get 404 instead of 403 to prevent job ID guessing

Responses:

  • 202: Accepted – Job successfully transitioned to 'cancelled' state
  • 200: OK – Job already in terminal state (cancelled, finished, or failed). Returns current status
  • 400: Bad Request – Invalid job_id format (must be UUID)
  • 401: Unauthorized – Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 404: Not Found – Job doesn't exist, or you don't have permission to cancel it

Examples:

# Cancel a job
curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8000/v1/jobs/123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000 \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

# Response (first time): 202 Accepted
# {"id": "123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000", "status": "cancelled"}

# Response (retry): 200 OK
# {"id": "123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000", "status": "cancelled"}

jobs.title: Why we need this endpoint:
jobs.descriptionHTML:
GET /v1/jobs/{job_id}/events – Real-time job progress via Server-Sent Events (SSE)

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Real-time updates: Users get instant notifications when job status changes, avoiding constant polling.
  • Better UX: Front-end apps can show live progress bars, status updates, and completion notifications.
  • Network efficiency: Single persistent connection is more efficient than polling every second.
  • Reliable delivery: Resume capability ensures clients don't miss events even after disconnections.
  • Without this endpoint, users would need to poll repeatedly, wasting bandwidth and missing instant updates.

What it does:

  • Opens a persistent HTTP connection that streams job updates in real-time
  • Sends events when job status changes (queued → running → finished/failed/cancelled)
  • Includes heartbeats every 15 seconds to keep connection alive
  • Automatically closes after job reaches terminal state (finished/failed/cancelled)

Access:

  • Job owner can stream their own jobs
  • Admin users with admin:all permission can stream any job
  • Other users get 404 Not Found (anti-enumeration)

Behavior:

  • Protocol: Standard Server-Sent Events (text/event-stream). Works with EventSource API in browsers
  • Resume: Send Last-Event-ID header to resume from last received event (uses ring buffer, 100 events)
  • Retry: Server sends retry: 5000 (5s default, configurable via ?retry_ms=3000 query param)
  • Heartbeats: Comment lines : heartbeat <n> every 15s while job is active
  • Terminal: After final status event, server sends event: end and closes connection
  • Backlog: If you missed too many events (ring buffer rotated), server sends : no-backlog-replay-from <id> comment
  • Redis backend: Events stored in Redis (durable, works across multiple servers). Recommended for production
  • Memory backend: Events stored in-process (single-server only, lost on restart)

Responses:

  • 200: OK – SSE stream established (content-type: text/event-stream)
  • 400: Bad Request – Invalid job_id (not UUID) or retry_ms out of range (1000-60000)
  • 401: Unauthorized – Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 404: Not Found – Job doesn't exist, or you don't have permission
  • 406: Not Acceptable – Client explicitly requested wrong content type (must accept text/event-stream)

Examples:

# Stream events (keeps connection open)
curl -N http://localhost:8000/v1/jobs/123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000/events \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

# With custom retry interval
curl -N "http://localhost:8000/v1/jobs/123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000/events?retry_ms=10000" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

# Resume from event ID 42
curl -N http://localhost:8000/v1/jobs/123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000/events \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -H "Last-Event-ID: 42"

# Example output:
# retry: 5000
# id: 1
# event: status
# data: {"job_id": "123e4567...", "status": "running"}
#
# : heartbeat 1
# id: 2
# event: end
# data: {"job_id": "123e4567...", "final": "finished"}

jobs.title: Why we need this endpoint:
jobs.descriptionHTML:
GET /v1/admin/jobs – List all users' jobs (admin only)

Why we need this endpoint:

  • System monitoring: Admins need visibility into all background jobs across all users to monitor system health.
  • Debugging: Helps identify stuck jobs, failed operations, or patterns of user issues.
  • Resource management: Shows which jobs are consuming resources and helps plan capacity.
  • Support: Enables admin team to investigate user-reported problems with specific jobs.
  • Without this endpoint, admins would have no way to see system-wide job activity or help users troubleshoot.

What it does:

  • Returns jobs from all users and tenants (system-wide visibility)
  • Supports filtering by status and pagination
  • Includes caching to reduce load when monitoring

Access:

  • Requires admin:all permission
  • Regular users get 403 Forbidden
  • Use regular /v1/jobs to see only your own jobs

Behavior:

  • Filtering: Add ?status=running or ?status=queued&status=running to filter results
  • Pagination: Results are sorted newest first (default 25 per page, max 50). Use next_page_token from response to get more
  • Caching: Returns ETag header. Send it back as If-None-Match to get 304 Not Modified when nothing changed
  • Scope: Shows all jobs regardless of owner (admin oversight)

Responses:

  • 200: OK – Job list with pagination info (items, total, has_more, next_page_token)
  • 304: Not Modified – No changes since your last request (when using If-None-Match)
  • 400: Bad Request – Invalid page_token (must be numeric offset like '0', '25')
  • 401: Unauthorized – Missing or invalid authentication token
  • 403: Forbidden – Requires admin:all permission

Examples:

# List all jobs (admin view)
curl -X GET http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/jobs \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"

     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"

curl -X GET http://localhost:8000/v1/admin/jobs \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
     -H "If-None-Match: W/\"abc123\""

jobs.descriptionHTML:
POST /v1/admin/jobs – Create a job on behalf of a user (admin only)

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Admin testing: Admins need to test job processing and debug issues without switching user accounts.
  • Support operations: Enables support staff to trigger jobs for users during troubleshooting.
  • System maintenance: Allows admins to start background tasks for system maintenance or data migration.
  • Testing & QA: Simplifies testing by letting admins create jobs without simulating user authentication.

  • Creates a background job using the same logic as /v1/jobs

  • Returns job ID and status immediately (doesn't wait for completion)

  • Auto-deduplication: Identical payloads are deduplicated within 24h window
  • Job types: Must be in allowed list (e.g., 'demo', 'test')
  • Retention: Jobs auto-expire (Redis: 10 days, Memory: 7 days)
  • Forwarding: This endpoint forwards to /v1/jobs implementation

jobs.title: Why we need this endpoint:
jobs.descriptionHTML:
DELETE /v1/admin/jobs/{job_id} – Cancel any user's job (admin only)

Why we need this endpoint:

  • Emergency control: Admins need ability to stop runaway or problematic jobs from any user.
  • System health: Enables cancelling resource-intensive jobs that are degrading system performance.
  • Support operations: Allows support staff to cancel stuck jobs during user support sessions.
  • Resource management: Helps free up worker capacity by stopping unnecessary jobs.
  • Without this endpoint, admins would have no way to intervene and stop problematic jobs, risking system stability.

What it does:

  • Cancels a background job owned by any user (system-wide access)
  • First successful cancel returns 202 Accepted, subsequent calls return 200 OK
  • Safe to retry (idempotent) – won't cause errors if already cancelled or finished

Access:

  • Requires admin:all permission
  • Can cancel jobs owned by any user (admin override)
  • Regular users should use /v1/jobs/{job_id} to cancel their own jobs

Behavior:

  • Idempotency: First cancel returns 202, all subsequent calls return 200 (safe to retry)
  • Terminal states: Already finished/failed/cancelled jobs return 200 with current status
  • Atomicity: Redis backend uses atomic Lua script for race-free cancellation
  • Forwarding: This endpoint forwards to /v1/jobs/{job_id} implementation with admin access

Responses:

  • 202: Accepted – Job successfully transitioned to 'cancelled' state
